t.1.34.1: Having passed the remainder of the night on the bank of the Śoṇā with the great sages, Viśvāmitra spoke when the night had brightened into a fair dawn.
t.1.34.2: The night has passed into a fair dawn, Rāma, and the morning twilight is setting in. Arise, arise, good fortune be with you; resolve upon departure.
t.1.34.3: Having heard those words of his and having performed the morning rites, he resolved upon departure and spoke these words.
t.1.34.4: This Śoṇa, with its pure waters, is fordable and adorned with sandbanks. By which path, O Brahman, shall we cross it?
t.1.34.5: Thus addressed by Rāma, Viśvāmitra said this: "This is the path I have pointed out, by which the great sages go."
t.1.34.6: Having travelled a long way, when half the day had passed, they then beheld the Jāhnavī, best of rivers, frequented by sages.
t.1.34.7: Seeing that river of holy waters, frequented by geese and cranes, all the sages, together with the Rāghavas, were delighted. Then they took up their lodging on its bank.
t.1.34.9: With joyful hearts they settled on the pure bank of the Jāhnavī, surrounding the great-souled Viśvāmitra on every side.
t.1.34.8: Then, having bathed according to rule and satisfied the ancestors and the gods with libations, having offered the agnihotra oblations into the fire and partaken of the sacrificial offering as though it were amṛta,
t.1.34.10: Then Rāma, his mind filled with delight, said to Viśvāmitra: "Blessed one, I wish to hear about the river Gaṅgā, who flows by three paths, and how she traversed the three worlds and went to the lord of rivers and streams."
t.1.34.11: Urged by the words of Rāma, the great sage Viśvāmitra began to tell of the birth and the growth of Gaṅgā.
t.1.34.12: There is a lord of mountains named Himavān, a great mine of minerals. He had two daughters, O Rāma, unequalled in beauty upon the earth.
t.1.34.13: O Rāma, the mother of those two was the slender-waisted daughter of Meru, Menā by name, charming indeed, the beloved wife of Himavant.
t.1.34.14: In her was born this Gaṅgā, the eldest daughter of Himavat; and his second daughter, O Rāghava, was the maiden named Umā.
t.1.34.15: Then all the gods, wishing to accomplish the purpose of the deities, asked the lord of mountains for his eldest daughter, Gaṅgā, the river that flows along three paths.
t.1.34.16: In accordance with dharma, Himavān gave his daughter Gaṅgā, the purifier of the worlds, who moves along whatever path she wills, out of a desire for the welfare of the three worlds.
t.1.34.17: Having received her for the sake of the three worlds, they, the benefactors of the three worlds, took Gaṅgā and departed with their inner selves fulfilled of their purpose.
t.1.34.18: And the other daughter of the mountain, the maiden, O Raghunandana, undertook a fierce vow and practised austerities, rich in penance.
t.1.34.19: The best of mountains gave his daughter Umā, endowed with fierce austerity and revered by the worlds, to the incomparable Rudra.
t.1.34.20: These are the two daughters of the king of mountains, revered by the world: Gaṅgā, the best of rivers, and the goddess Umā, O Rāghava.
t.1.34.21: This sacred account has been told to you, dear child, best of those who move: how the river Tripathagā first took her course and went to the sky.
